messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 26
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Maid
- Trauma Type: Torture
- Pcl5: 73

He is 26, Latin American, and works as a maid in a hotel, moving quietly through other people’s messes while trying not to take up space himself. He comes to therapy divorced and carrying a kind of vigilance that never fully turns off. The story he tells begins with torture, though he struggles at first to name it that way. He describes it instead as a time when his body stopped belonging to him.

Before the trauma, he is already used to hard work and instability. He has learned early to keep his head down, to avoid attention, to be useful. When he is detained and tortured, those old habits turn into survival strategies that no longer protect him. He remembers the first blow as a moment when the world narrows to sound and pain. After that, the details come in fragments: the smell of sweat and dirt, the harsh light, hands forcing him into positions his body cannot sustain, his own voice cracking when he tries to answer. He says that during those hours he feels himself splitting in two — one part enduring, the other floating above the scene, watching from a distance because staying inside the pain would be unbearable.

When he is finally released, he expects relief, but instead he notices that fear follows him home. He cannot sit with his back to a door. He checks locks repeatedly, then checks them again because once is never enough. He sleeps lightly, waking at small sounds, his heart already racing before he is fully conscious. At night, his body remembers before his mind does. A smell, a slammed door, footsteps in a hallway, or the sudden pressure of being touched unexpectedly can send him back into the same helpless panic. In those moments he is not in his room or at work; he is back in the place where pain was used to make him submit.

He tries to continue with life because there is no other option. He finds work cleaning hotel rooms, a job that suits his need for control in small, manageable spaces. He likes that the tasks are clear: make the bed, wipe the counters, empty the trash, move on. The predictability helps, but even there he is never fully relaxed. He scans every hallway, listens for raised voices, and startles when a guest opens a door too quickly. He prefers to work alone if he can. When he has to enter a room, he stands near the exit without thinking about it. He notices that he becomes irritated when beds are left in disarray or when someone makes a mess and expects him to clean it. The resentment is not really about the mess; it is about the feeling that other people can leave behind chaos and walk away while he has to contain it.

His marriage does not survive the aftermath. He says he wanted his wife to understand why he became distant, but he did not know how to explain that being held, questioned, or even simply watched could make his skin crawl. He withdraws rather than risk being seen in pain. Intimacy becomes difficult, and then impossible. He is ashamed of the way his body reacts — the tension, the numbness, the sudden panic — and he starts to believe that he has become less of a man. The divorce leaves him feeling like a failure, but also oddly relieved, because constant effort to hide his fear had been exhausting.

He avoids anything that might stir memory: news about detention, conversations about politics, even certain movies. He does not like to be alone with his thoughts for too long because the mind has a way of opening doors he has spent years trying to keep closed. When the memories come, they arrive with sensory force rather than narrative order. He remembers the texture of the floor, the sound of breathing near his ear, the humiliation more than the sequence of events. Sometimes he becomes so tense that his jaw aches for hours. Other times he feels strangely empty, as if the part of him that reacts has gone somewhere else.

Despite all this, he keeps working, pays his bills, and shows up on time. People often mistake his quietness for calm. In sessions, he speaks in a low, careful voice, as though choosing each word for safety. Over time, he begins to admit that he is tired of living as if danger is always one step behind him. Even in the telling, he keeps one part of himself alert, listening for what might happen next.
